https://www.fox2detroit.com/news/andrew-.text: article Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan Tate talk to the media outside their residence on March 23, 2025 in Bucharest, Romania. (Photo by Andrei Pungovschi/Getty Images) Expand The Brief Andrew and Tristan Tate will fight extradition to the U.K. following their arrest in Miami over the weekend. British prosecutors recently filed new rape and sex trafficking charges against them related to investigations involving four victims. The pair already face similar charges in the UK in cases that involved multiple other victims. Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate plan to fight being sent to the United Kingdom where they face a host of rape and sex trafficking charges. Big picture view: The brothers were detained in Miami over the weekend and appeared in a federal court for the first time on Monday as a judge weighs whether they meet the conditions to be extradited. The Tate brothers’ attorney, Joseph McBride, told the court that his clients should not be sent to the U.K. to stand trial because "they’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit." Lawyer suggests political motivation McBride also hinted at the Tates’ arrests being politically motivated, telling reporters that "there’s no question about it." He alleged his clients’ case was a big factor in the recent fall of British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, although he did not say how. McBride also indicated that the brothers were arrested after meeting "friends in Washington, D.C." Again, though, he was light on details when it came to who they may have met or why. The charges The Tate brothers had already faced rape, human trafficking, and other charges relating to allegations by three women regarding events that occurred between 2012 and 2015 in North London, when prosecutors revealed even more charges Saturday in connection with four more victims. Including prior charges, Andrew Tate, 39, now faces a total of 10 counts of rape. Among the new allegations against him are three related to sex trafficking, three of assault, and 19 for offenses connected to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Tristan Tate, 38, faces two more counts of rape, in addition to the three already filed against him. The other new charges include a single count of sexual assault, and three counts related to sex trafficking, prosecutors said. Dig deeper: The brothers, who are former professional kick-boxers, are proponents of hypermasculinity and have gained millions of followers, particularly among young men and boys, by advocating a life of luxury and misogyny. The Tate brothers are dual U.S. and British citizens and moved to Romania in 2016, where they were arrested six years later on allegations of sexual exploitation. They denied the charges and the cases ended up not going forward because of legal and procedural irregularities. The Source: Information for this article was taken from The Associated Press and previous coverage. This story was reported from Orlando. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-satel.text: The European Commission is ready to offer “eyes in the sky” via the Copernicus program to support Indonesian search and rescue operations after the country was hit by a 7.7 magnitude earthquake, President Ursula von der Leyen said Saturday . “Indonesia, we stand with you,” von der Leyen said in a post on X. Copernicus is an observation system that can provide mapping services useful for search operations and damage assessments. Advertisement Advertisement At least 38 people have died since the powerful quake struck the island of Flores, the BBC reported citing a press conference by Indonesia’s disaster response agency. Rescue operations are ongoing . The foreign ministries of Italy , Greece and Estonia and officials have posted messages of support on X today. Earlier this week, the Commission provided €2.1 million for assistance in Colombia as well as use of the Copernicus system after it was hit by a 7.4 magnitude quake.

https://www.dw.com/en/why-starlink-won-t.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JM87 Vietnam already has high mobile network coverage, but information is tightly controlled Image: Nhac Nguyen/AFP Advertisement Elon Musk's Starlink has begun selling satellite internet in Vietnam, bringing its high-speed service to one of the world's most tightly controlled online environments . The satellite internet service operated by Musk's SpaceX began accepting orders from Vietnamese customers this month, with residential packages starting at around €37 ($43) a month. Vietnam's government announced in March 2025 that it would allow SpaceX to launch Starlink on a controlled trial basis, waiving the usual restrictions on foreign ownership. The trial is capped at 600,000 subscribers and is due to run until the end of 2030. The service is operated through Starlink Services Vietnam, a local SpaceX subsidiary established last September. Vietnamese authorities subsequently licensed four ground gateway stations and up to 600,000 Starlink terminals for the initial rollout. The gateways allow satellite traffic to connect with terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure inside Vietnam. Vietnam authorized the trial in March 2025 as it sought to head off threatened US trade measures over its large bilateral trade surplus. At the time, some analysts viewed approval of Starlink, alongside tariff reductions on several US products, as part of Hanoi's effort to ease trade tensions with Washington. Starlink comes at a high cost Vietnam officially connected to the global internet in 1997. By the end of 2025, it had around 85.6 million internet users, equivalent to 84.2% of the population, according to government data. Conventional internet infrastructure is already extensive. Around 85% of Vietnamese households had fiber-optic internet, while there were more than 110 million mobile broadband subscriptions, and the country's 5G network covered around 92% of the population, according to official statistics. Starlink is relatively expensive compared to other network options, but its most obvious advantage is not in well-connected cities such as Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City but in mountainous, remote and island communities where terrestrial infrastructure remains weaker. The Vietnamese government says Starlink could help increase internet access in remote areas, islands and places without adequate terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure. Because satellite connections rely less on local cables and towers, they could also provide backup communications when terrestrial networks are damaged by typhoons, floods or landslides. However, Starlink currently advertises its cheapest household plan in Vietnam at about €37 a month, while the necessary hardware starts at roughly €284. In rural areas, where Starlink could potentially be most useful, average monthly income is just €259, according to Vietnam's National Statistics Office. "Without subsidies, it will be unaffordable for many rural households. Its greatest impact may therefore come through shared connections for institutions such as schools, clinics and local government offices rather than individual subscriptions," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW. Freedom online: Who's negotiating it? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Connectivity without internet freedom Whatever Starlink does for connectivity, there is little indication that its arrival will loosen Vietnam's increasingly tight control of online speech . Freedom House's 2025 Freedom on the Net report gave Vietnam a score of just 22 out of 100 and classified the country's internet as "not free." Among the Asia-Pacific countries assessed, only China and Myanmar scored lower. And foreign technology companies are already central to enforcing those restrictions. Vietnamese authorities said Facebook, YouTube and TikTok complied with more than 94% of government requests to remove or block content during the first half of 2026. Human Rights Watch and other rights groups have repeatedly criticized foreign platforms for facilitating state censorship. In previous years, Hanoi publicly reported compliance rates of around 90% or higher for requests made to Facebook and YouTube to remove content the government considered illegal or anti-state. The 2025 decision approving the Starlink pilot made clear from the outset that connectivity would remain subordinate to state security concerns, with the telecoms ministry stating that the "programme will adhere to national security and defence principles," according to the news website VNExpress. Starlink must play by Vietnam's rules Vietnam has also steadily expanded the legal tools available to police the internet . Decree 147, which took effect in December 2024, requires social media companies to verify users, hand over certain data and remove content deemed illegal by the authorities within 24 hours. A new Cybersecurity Law took effect in July, further consolidating state control over cyberspace. New implementing regulations issued on August 19 allow authorities to demand that online content be removed within 24 hours and provide for accounts to be restricted or blocked for repeated violations. The law also for the first time explicitly refers to constructing a "national firewall" to counter cybersecurity threats. "As Vietnam is an interesting market for Starlink and the service is on a trial period, the company will ensure that it sticks to the governmental regulations rather than offering the Vietnamese citizens technical options to circumvent censorship," Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Southeast Asia at the University of Vienna, told DW. Starlink must operate through a Vietnamese company and licensed domestic gateway stations, meaning that its service is not being introduced as a parallel internet infrastructure beyond the reach of Vietnamese regulators. An analysis by the Singapore Space Agency last month noted that Starlink in Vietnam, unlike in most other Southeast Asian countries, will be channeled through four domestic gateway earth stations and supervised jointly by the Ministry of Science and Technology, the Ministry of National Defence and the Ministry of Public Security. "Vietnamese instinct is risk containment through enclosure," the report noted. According to Gerstl, "Starlink will not open a breach in the Bamboo Firewall," a reference to the nickname for Vietnam's system of legal restrictions, content controls and technical measures to regulate the internet. "The regime will continue to uphold digital sovereignty. Indeed, censorship, currently less strict than in China, is expected to be further expanded in the future," he added. Starlink may provide Vietnamese users with another way to get online, but it does not provide them with an internet beyond the reach of the Vietnamese state. At best, said Giang, Starlink may broaden access to information for communities that previously had poor connectivity, which is beneficial in itself, "but better connectivity does not necessarily mean greater freedom of speech," he added. https://www.politico.eu/article/berlin-l.text: Getting into Gideon Joffe’s office takes some doing. Above the historic building in the heart of Berlin rises the golden dome of the New Synagogue, built in the 19th century. Out front, police officers ask who you are and where you’re headed. Past the first security door, your bag goes through a scanner. Then come more doors, all of them extra thick. It’s not paranoia. Since the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Hamas and the outbreak of the war in Gaza, antisemitism has surged across the Western world, according to a study by Tel Aviv University. Berlin — where senior Nazi officials gathered at a lakeside villa in 1942 to coordinate the murder of Europe’s Jews — is no exception. Joffe, 54, who chairs the Jewish Community of Berlin, one of Germany’s largest, has grown used to a life under protection. For decades, such security has been a fact of Jewish life across Europe, with synagogues and schools fortified and, in many cities, guarded by armed police. But the situation has rarely been as bad as it is now, he tells me. Advertisement The Tel Aviv-born former businessman does not come across as a timid man: a firm handshake, a shirt straining at every seam and a deep and penetrating voice. Yet the mood at his conference table, where the community’s secretary general and its spokesperson also sit, is one of great concern. The subject of that concern: The result of the recent Berlin election, in which the Left Party — a successor to the communist party that ruled East Germany until 1989 — came in first with 26% of the vote. It’s a record for the party in the capital, and more than double its previous result. Germany has been arguing about the consequences ever since. Among the trio sitting at the table, the Left Party’s Berlin branch is seen as not just radically left-wing but also a hotbed of antisemitism. The party made opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza a central plank of its election campaign. While some Jews have declared their support for the Left, leading Jewish institutions have criticized it. Elif Eralp, lead candidate of the far-left Die Linke, taking a selfie with a fan while campaigning in Marzahn district ahead of Berlin state elections on September 15, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images At the center of the debate is Elif Eralp, the Left’s lead candidate in the Berlin election who has become the face of the party’s transformation. Under Eralp and a younger generation of activists, many with immigrant backgrounds in the Muslim world, the party has expanded well beyond its East German roots and built a new urban coalition around housing, inequality and opposition to the war in Gaza. Eralp and other prominent Left officials concede there have been troubling incidents among their supporters, and have condemned them. At a party conference shortly after the election, Eralp pledged to “strengthen the diverse Jewish life in Berlin and combat antisemitism.” It was an acknowledgment of an issue that has been central to her effort to become mayor. In Germany, a single party is rarely strong enough to rule alone; forming a government means weeks of haggling among parties that dislike each other to varying degrees. If Eralp is to govern, she will need to form a coalition with the center-left Social Democrats and the Greens. Among their demands: “combating antisemitism and protecting Jewish life,” according to a joint statement by the two parties . Advertisement “There needs to be a binding agreement that not only condemns antisemitism and affirms Israel’s right to exist, but also stipulates clear consequences for antisemitic incidents,” SPD state chair Steffen Krach told the German press agency dpa . The Left’s new face “Elif! Elif! Elif!” As the petite woman in the black bomber jacket enters the hall, her comrades rise from their chairs and chant her name in rhythm. “Elif for Berlin,” read the banners in big, bright red letters. Her first major appearance since the Sept. 20 election is in a small hall at the headquarters of Neues Deutschland, a newspaper that once served as the official mouthpiece of East Germany’s communist dictatorship. Eralp — a 45-year-old lawyer, mother of two and the daughter of Turkish socialists who fled to Germany in 1980, the year of a military coup in Turkey — is the new star of Germany’s hard left. She has thrilled young women and Muslim voters in droves. Her plea for economic justice, especially on Berlin’s crowded housing market, is what won the election, say her supporters. Critics say her success mainly depended on mobilizing pro-Palestinian activists, including some sharply hostile to Israel. Elif Eralp speaks to the media the day after state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on September 21, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images Eralp has been dubbed “Berlin’s Mamdani” by the press, and the comparison is more than cosmetic. Berlin’s Left borrowed from New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s playbook, right down to the political strategist who helped engineer his success: Morris Katz, a 27-year-old consultant who helped steer Mamdani to victory and flew to Berlin to coach Eralp this spring. “If a leftist can win in New York, then one can just as well win in Berlin,” Eralp said after Mamdani’s 2025 election. Where Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, promised city-owned grocery stores, Eralp promises neighborhood canteens with meals from €3. She wants a rent cap for the Berlin’s publicly owned housing and the “socialization” of big corporate landlords, taking public control of more than 200,000 apartments — which a majority of Berliners backed in a 2021 referendum. Mamdani had his potholes; Eralp has Berlin’s “garbage chaos.” Both have proven that rent bills and trash cans can win big-city elections. And both have had to rebut the same accusation of antisemitism, either personally or within their ranks. Advertisement Mamdani — a fierce critic of Israel who has called for the country’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to be arrested — spent his campaign declining to condemn the slogan “globalize the intifada,” while saying he doesn’t use it himself and that it pains him to be called an antisemite. He eventually said he would discourage use of the phrase. Zohran Mamdani waves on stage at CultureCon 2026 in New York City on Oct. 03, 2026. | John Nacion/Getty Images Since taking office, Mamdani has also sought to address the concerns of Jewish New Yorkers. In late September, he announced his city’s first municipal strategy to combat antisemitism, vowing that Jews in the city would be “safe and celebrated.” Eralp, who like Mamdani calls herself a “democratic socialist,” faces similar skepticism from much of her city’s Jewish community. While international debate about antisemitism in the country has focused on the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany party, since the election in Berlin, the controversy has centered on the Left. The party’s Berlin platform explicitly opposes antisemitism, but Eralp’s critics are not interested in what’s on paper. Instead, they point to an unofficial picture assembled from numerous examples: a campaign poster demanding “Freedom for Palestine”; the Berlin youth wing of the party that attributes a “colonial and racist character” to the “Israeli state project”; a rapper who shouted “Yalla yalla intifada” and “Death, death to the IDF” — Israel’s army — at a campaign event; and the appearance of a leading supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, an EU- and U.S.-designated terrorist organization, at a Left victory party in Berlin. Opposition to Israel’s policies in Gaza is not the same as antisemitism, and Eralp has condemned the appearances of the rapper and the PFLP supporter, blaming local party officials. But that hasn’t convinced her critics. Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, has dismissed her expressions of concern about antisemitism as “lip service.” Balancing act Nowhere in Berlin has the Left changed more than in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, a borough of about 267,000 people. For decades, it was a stronghold of the Green Party. This time the Left won 44% there, more than double its previous result. The local party used to be run by old-school socialists, many of them veterans of the Socialist Unity Party, or SED, which ruled East Germany as a one-party dictatorship until the Berlin Wall fell in 1989. Advertisement Today, it is driven by young activists who have expanded the party’s base into immigrant communities, above all among young Muslims. For many of them, the principles that have guided German politics since the Holocaust — the duty to protect Jewish life and solidarity with Israel — carry little weight, and some reject them outright. That leaves Eralp with a delicate balancing act: reassuring Jewish Berliners concerned about elements of her party while holding together the coalition that helped propel it to victory. In her first major speech after the election, she tried to do both. The Left’s vision of an affordable and good life, she said to applause, had been stronger “than all attacks and stronger than the hatred.” She would not be showered with insults by the “most unpopular chancellor of all time” — a swipe at Merz — and other politicians in the federal government. Israel supporters hold Israel national flag as people march to commemorate the 78th anniversary of the Nakba on May 16, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. | Michele Tantussi/Getty Images These centrist politicians, Eralp continued, were dividing the country, cutting labor rights and pensions and adopting the anti-migrant positions of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), the far-right party on track to secure its first state government after a breakthrough election last month . “While a fascist party in Saxony-Anhalt is on its way to power, these people seriously think they can stop a democratic party that stands for social justice, diversity and democracy with this smear campaign,” she said. Next, Eralp presented an offer of reconciliation: The point was to “build bridges and bring people back together.” Then she offered a kind of self-criticism, but without getting specific. The Left, too, she said, must be clear “that there must never be calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people can never come from our platforms.” Here, too, there was applause. But quite a few listeners had their arms folded. Some wore Palestinian scarves, known as keffiyehs, around their necks. Advertisement Eralp was not available after the party meeting, and her party’s co-chair, Ines Schwerdtner, declined an interview. “Leave this country” Michael Wolffsohn has grim advice for Jewish Berliners. The prominent historian and conservative commentator was born in Tel Aviv to a family of Jewish merchants from Berlin, who fled the Nazis for Palestine in 1939. As a boy, he came back with his parents to West Berlin. In the magazine Cicero, Wolffsohn, 79, said what he would tell a young Jewish Berliner who asks whether to stay: with a heavy heart, “Leave this city and this country.” He himself, he added, was too old to uproot. Were he younger, he, too, would leave. It is not hard to see why Berlin’s estimated 20,000 to 40,000 Jews are on edge. In the five years before the 2023 Hamas attack in Israel and the resulting war in Gaza, RIAS Berlin, a watchdog that tracks antisemitic incidents in the city whether or not they are crimes, logged just under 1,000 a year. Last year it counted 2,197 . The police recorded an even steeper increase in crimes classified as antisemitic: from 381 in 2022 to 2,268 in 2025. RIAS follows the definition of antisemitism laid out by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, counting conduct ranging from insults and graffiti to statements at demonstrations. It says it did not simply count criticism of Israel’s conduct in Gaza or of the Israeli military as antisemitic, but did so when the situation in Gaza was used to disparage Jews collectively, justify violence against them or trivialize the Holocaust. Some incidents were violent. RIAS recorded 39 physical attacks in Berlin last year, 16 of them in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg. RIAS says multiple people who reported antisemitic incidents described becoming more cautious in daily life, including no longer openly wearing Jewish symbols after repeated harassment. Advertisement A volunteer attaches portraits of Israelis killed since the October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas at a commemorative installation in front of the Brandenburg Gate on the second anniversary of the attack on October 07, 2025 in Berlin, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images Speaking to POLITICO on the phone, Wolffsohn details his concerns: “Elif Eralp is the party’s star. But there is a broad base, and that’s what matters.” Is the Left fit to govern the capital? His answer is categorical: “Is such a party capable of fulfilling the elementary task of a state — protecting its citizens, and not only the Jewish ones, at home and abroad? My answer is: No, absolutely not. The Left does not disqualify itself through opinions but through its demonstrable activities.” Wolffsohn says he wouldn’t take a coalition contract at its word. Or a potential agreement that would commit all partners to fight antisemitism. “Paper is patient,” he says, using a German proverb: Paper will accept anything written on it. At the moment, there isn’t even paper. Berlin’s leaders of the Left, the Social Democrats and the Greens have been meeting over the past week in “constructive” preliminary talks. They are gathering for a third round Wednesday, but have not yet agreed on a common line on antisemitism. The trust test Joffe, the chair of Berlin’s Jewish Community, extends the blame for rising antisemitism to Germany’s mainstream parties, which he says failed to tackle the problem. “I don’t know a single Jewish community member who is sure that his children or grandchildren will still be living in Germany.” A 2024 survey of more than 2,500 Jews across Germany found that more than half considered it unsafe to live visibly as a Jew in their city, while three-quarters said they felt less safe since Oct. 7, 2023. In his heavily secured office, Joffe says he understands why many people find Eralp likeable. “She’s nobody’s fool, and she knows how to express herself,” he tells me. “But the antisemitic spirits in her party — she probably won’t be able to get them back into the bottle.” Advertisement Joffe often pauses to choose his words carefully. “There have been many statements from the Left Party that have unsettled the Jewish community,” he says. “But I don’t want the issue of antisemitism alone to decide whether a coalition comes together in Berlin or not. Then conspiracy theories will just resurface that we Jews are so powerful we can even help decide who governs this city.” His test for Eralp’s party is less about what the Left promises than about what happens in the capital in the coming years, especially in schools and kindergartens. The Left’s Berlin platform promises to fight antisemitism “effectively,” but also warns against the “instrumentalization” of antisemitism allegations. Joffe worries that its broader law-and-order agenda — including proposals to reduce police staffing, curb police resources and loosen restrictions on masked protesters — would make it harder to contain antisemitic intimidation and violence. RIAS recorded antisemitic incidents at a record 239 rallies and marches last year. That’s four or five a week. On Sept. 27, 2025, the Left was among the groups that called for a Gaza march that drew up to 100,000 people. RIAS documented antisemitic incidents at the march and rally that followed, including placards equating Israel’s war with the Holocaust and chants of “child murderers” — language the watchdog says either trivializes the Nazis’ industrial-scale murder of six million Jews or draws on the centuries-old antisemitic blood-libel trope
